speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Yet, cost of living pressures can also be an expression of the gap between one’s aspirations and one's anticipated means to fulfil them.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Different groups of Singaporeans have different concerns, needs and wants.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Elderly Singaporeans, retirees and their families will be more concerned with healthcare affordability.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Families with young children and infants may be more concerned about the prices of milk powder and educational programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Yet other families may be aspiring to buy their dream house or car.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: Furthermore, we are also aware that some price items, while not the biggest in absolute impact, can have a disproportionate psychological impact on consumers.

speaker: The Minister for Trade and Industry (Mr Chan Chun Sing)
text: For example, water and transport fares fall into this category because they are items consumed daily.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In fact, inflation over the past five years between 2012 and 2017, at an average of +0.6% a year, was significantly lower than the preceding five years between 2007 and 2012, which averaged +4%.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we consider the CPI-All Items less imputed rental, the figure was 1.7% for 2017.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Beyond these numbers, I have also asked the Ministry of Trade and Industry to do a check on certain groups of households.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Specifically, I asked them to look at the retiree households.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For retiree households, the figure last year was -0.4%.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We know that inflation is a concern for retirees with no active income from work.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is why the Government has focused much attention on help schemes for our seniors, starting with the Pioneer Generation Package.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In addition to transport and healthcare subsidies for the elderly, we are also encouraged to see our social enterprises and businesses stepping up to help ease cost pressures on them by giving our seniors additional discounts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We also monitor the inflation for key categories of goods and services, for example, food, healthcare and utilities, because they can have a big psychological impact on the daily lived experience of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the graphs, Members will be able to see that the inflation rate was lower over the recent five-year period between 2012 and 2017 for all household types, as compared to the five-year period from 2007 to 2012.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Inflation rates were also lower for the key components of food, healthcare, and utilities and fuel for these household types.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, we should note the sharp pick-up in inflation rate for utilities and fuel last year, and this was largely due to higher oil prices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Last year, the oil price went from $50-plus per barrel to $70-plus per barrel – a significant increase.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, rising global oil prices are projected to increase fuel costs and electricity prices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This, coupled with an increase in global food commodity prices, could impact domestic food prices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Consumer prices could also rise moderately alongside a faster pace of wage growth and pickup in domestic demand amidst improvements in the labour market.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Accommodation costs are expected to continue to decline with a sustained fall in rentals, thereby dampening inflation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We closely monitor prices to ensure that Singapore remains an affordable home for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are some factors not within our control.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And there are other factors that we have to work hard to constantly manage.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a small and open economy that imports most of our items, we are subject to global economic forces.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Electricity and fuel costs which are influenced by global oil prices are one such example.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The prices of certain products are also affected by our market size.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Major companies determine their pricing strategies based on the purchasing power and relative bargaining power of different markets.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The price of certain medicine is one such example.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To manage the various pressure points, we must adopt a multi-pronged strategy.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: After this, I will distribute a set of infographics for Members to share with your residents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, we need to keep our economy competitive.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: At the macro level, the Government will aim to establish the conditions for companies to create good jobs with sustained income growth that outpaces inflation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Over the last five years, resident households’ income had risen faster than consumer price inflation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Median resident household income from work per member grew by 4.2% per annum in real terms between 2012 and 2017, while that for the lower income deciles rose between 4.2% and 4.6% per annum.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In the long run, real wage growth is determined by our ability to raise productivity.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Schemes, such as the Productivity Solutions Grant, aim to help companies to do so.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Other schemes like the Special Employment Credit support employment opportunities for low-income and older Singaporeans, while the Workfare Income Supplement (WIS) Scheme helps low-wage workers supplement their incomes and build up their retirement savings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We also need to constantly monitor the wages of workers in industries facing significant disruptions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The best way for us to help our workers facing low or stagnating wage growth is to equip them with new skills to take on new jobs ahead of time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is where schemes like Adapt and Grow come in to help our workers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We carefully manage our Reserves and the strength of our dollar to contain imported inflation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Monetary Authority of Singapore's (MAS’) exchange rate-centred monetary policy, through a gradual appreciation of the trade-weighted Singapore dollar in line with the economy’s underlying fundamentals, helps to preserve our purchasing power.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We do so from food and water to fuel and raw materials for production to ensure that we are not held ransom by any single source.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This bolsters the security and resilience of our resource supply chains, and avoid sharp price hikes when there are disruptions to our primary sources.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Fourth, promoting competition in our markets and lowering barriers to entry where possible, to allow Singaporeans to enjoy competitive prices for comparable products.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, the Energy Market Authority of Singapore (EMA) has progressively opened up the electricity market to competition since 2001.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Consumer feedback so far has been positive, with thirteen electricity retailers offering a good range of competitively priced plans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Another example is the market for mobile telecommunication services, where the Infocomm Media Development Authority's (IMDA’s) regulatory measures to facilitate greater competition in recent years have led to an increasingly vibrant and competitive mobile market.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: New mobile operators are offering competitive and innovative mobile plans, including plans that allow for unlimited data, or those that start from zero dollars.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Fifth, we must manage the cost of doing business in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We must continue to simplify our processes and reduce business costs to minimise the pass through of costs to consumers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: To keep domestic sources of inflation contained, we will continue to carefully manage domestic supply-side constraints.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For instance, the Government will ensure an adequate supply of residential, industrial and commercial space to relieve price and rental cost pressures as demand grows.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will also carefully monitor property market trends and take necessary actions to avoid sharp price changes that are not supported by market fundamentals.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: As a general principle, we price services fairly to recover costs and discourage over-consumption.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, our Government agencies are also frequently reminded and are committed to keeping our costs under control to avoid imposing additional burden on businesses and consumers.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Various agencies are now using the price-quality model for tender evaluations to moderate the excesses of pure price competition.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This can be seen in the case of new hawker centre tenders.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Since 2012, the National Environment Agency (NEA) has removed reserve rental in the tender for stalls in hawker centres, and 52% of stalls are awarded at bids below reserve rental today.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Another example is the Early Childhood Development Agency’s (ECDA's) use of the Anchor Operator and Partner Operator Schemes to provide quality early childhood care and education at affordable prices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Pro-Enterprise Panel will also work with businesses to find meaningful and effective ways to help lower regulatory costs for businesses, which include improving regulatory efficiency, simplifying processes and removing unnecessary licences.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Sixth, focusing our help schemes to do more for those with less.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is an accepted principle by most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we also understand that various groups of Singaporeans would like to see more being done for them, be it in the areas of education, housing, healthcare, transport or other policies.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Ultimately, we must forge a social consensus of how much we want to tax the general public to support the desired groups in a targeted manner.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, we do not subsidise electricity or petrol prices upfront.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That would disproportionately benefit wealthier households as they tend to consume more of such goods.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Instead, the Government provides U-Save rebates, with households living in smaller Housing and Development Board (HDB) flats getting a higher amount.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: While this strategy is economically and socially sound, it comes with two challenges.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, by not subsidising prices upfront, consumers may experience a "higher sticker price".

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This may create a disproportionate negative psychological impact because the backend subsidies to help lower-income groups reduce the actual prices paid, is not as obvious or visible.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, it is always politically more difficult to carry the ground when different groups of people receive varying levels of assistance because they are assessed to have different needs.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Regardless of the method of needs assessment, it will often be fraught with debate and challenged by those who receive relatively less help.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: However, the alternative to give the same help to all without discrimination also cannot be the wisest way to expend our finite resources to help those who need it most.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will work with the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) to strengthen CASE's capabilities to better promote consumer awareness and empower consumers to make informed purchasing choices to stretch their hard-earned dollar.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, with technology and crowd sourcing platforms, consumers should be much better able to make informed choices on where are the best deals in their local neighbourhoods.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Last but not least, our eighth strategy, leveraging our social enterprises.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government will continue to work with social enterprises like NTUC to benchmark the prices of various essentials.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This was the origin of the WELCOME supermarkets for groceries many years ago.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: NTUC Social Enterprises have, over the years, extended its offerings to include basic insurance, childcare, eldercare services and cooked food options to meet the evolving needs of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We should be getting a set of three.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There will be more of these in the Members' Room for Members who wish to have more copies to distribute to their residents to help reassure our residents that we will do what we can to help everyone manage their cost of living issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Cost of living pressures will always be present in various forms.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are many factors that drive price changes.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There are also real and perceived gaps between Singaporeans’ aspirations and anticipated means to fulfil these aspirations.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: More importantly, we recognise Singaporeans’ evolving aspirations for a better life for themselves and their families, and the associated stress of achieving real income growth in a volatile economic environment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The Government remains committed to helping all Singaporeans manage and achieve their aspirations.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am heartened that the Government is paying attention to this issue and harnessing the whole of Government, whole of society, to deal with this ongoing concern.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have a further question for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This group is unlikely to qualify for most of the schemes, or the subsidies are always often tiered lower due to their higher income.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Understandably, they do aspire to live well and they also want to have a better lifestyle, whether it is wants or needs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They are feeling that the household expenditures are also rising as their financial commitment increases.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Of course, as a general policy, we try to do more for those with lower income and, perhaps, the retirees first.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, the Government is very aware of the aspirations and the needs of the middle-income group.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why we have a broad-based swathe of measures that I have alluded to, to help everyone in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But specifically for the middle-income group, there are also various schemes that the Government will extend to help them.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It may not be in the same quantum as the lower-income group but, generally, they do get different forms of help and different tiers of help.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members might recall that, once upon a time, when I was in the Ministry of Social and Family Development (MSF), I showed everyone a chart, a diagram, which is now euphemistically known as the kueh lapis chart.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We try to help everyone in Singapore by making sure that those with the least get the most.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But that does not mean that those with more did not get anything.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is just a tiering of the different help schemes that they have.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, for many of the middle-income, I think their concerns would be the education for their children and, perhaps, the utilities bill that they have to face.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Also, many of them will be taking care of their elderly parents as well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are very aware of this and the way we help them is as follows.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, we try to do as much as we can to take care of our seniors to relieve the burden from the middle-income households with elderly parents.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, we want to make sure that the children's education remains affordable and everyone will have similar opportunities to excel and to fulfil their potential.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Our promise as a Government is that, so long someone is capable and committed, they need not worry about their means, their family's circumstances.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why we give away as many scholarships/bursary awards as possible to help our students excel.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, by relieving the pressures from the older folks and the younger folks, we hope to relieve the pressures on the middle-income middle-aged families.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Members would probably know that I came from a single-parent family, so my mother had to work two jobs when we were young, so I was brought up by my maternal grandmother.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: There were three things that I always remember her teaching me about managing our family's finances.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, she always reminded me that I must get a good job.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I must make sure that I earn enough to take care of the family.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is a reminder to urge us to study hard, to acquire the correct skills and that, so long as you are prepared to work hard, there will be an opportunity in Singapore for us to succeed.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And this is also the same philosophy and commitment that I bring with me to MTI, NTUC and MSF, that we must help our workers, first and foremost, to have those opportunities to realise their aspirations and ambitions.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The second lesson that my grandmother always drummed into us is that we should aim high.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Singaporeans, like all of us here – it is not a sin to aim high.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We should all aim high but yet, at the same time, we must know our own strengths and weaknesses so that we do not stress ourselves or overly stress ourselves and our families.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We must know what our capabilities are, what we are good at.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But as we aim high, we must also be realistic in how we achieve those ambitions, like the Chinese say 适可而止 – knowing our own limits.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The third thing that my grandmother always reminded me was that, regardless of our family's circumstances, we must always have a care for those who are less fortunate than us and who may need a bit more help than us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: During my time, I never knew that there was something called "MPS" – to go and see the Member of Parliament (MP).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We did not have Social Service Offices (SSOs).

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We had 福利部 but I was always reminded that, that is really for those who really, really need help and we should always try to take care of ourselves and, at the same time, take care of other people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I think these three rules are quite instructive in how we approach this issue of cost of living.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, we must make sure that every Singaporean has good jobs that can allow them to fulfil their potential.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Second, we must help Singaporeans stretch their hard-earned dollar, that while pursuing their ambitions and aspirations, that we are also realistic about our options and how we should distinguish the needs and the wants, so that our families can have a better quality of life that is sustainable.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Because it shows that there is a decline from 2007 until 2017.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But then, if you are to look at the price at the coffee shop, it is definitely not the trend.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And each increase in the food price is a lot.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Please do not ask my residents to go to CASE, because it affects all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is actually a valuable opportunity for me to clarify some things.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would not speak on behalf of NTUC FairPrice.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I would share my experience as a previous and immediate-past NTUC Secretary-General.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The way to read the chart is that it is not that the food prices are decreasing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It is an increase but a slower rate of increase.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why I mentioned at the beginning of my speech, some of the food items and the prices will have a disproportionate impact because, in our psychological perception, we use it every day.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, coffee prices at coffee shops will be one very clear example.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But in the overall basket of goods, coffee is but one item in a basket of goods.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, how a basket of goods is constituted statistically is by the spending pattern of the different household types.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Different household types have different baskets of goods.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the first clarification is that it is not that the prices are not increasing, but they are increasing at a different rate and it also depends on the basket of goods if you look at the charts, for example, in the top chart.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why we have broken it down into the bottom 20%, middle 60% and top 20%.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Each of the three groups, including the retiree households, also have a different basket of goods because their consumption patterns are different.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you set up a committee to go and look at coffee price in one coffee shop, and there will be many of these places, the speed is just not fast enough.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And you ask a committee to decide whether the price is fair or not, it is also quite difficult.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But today, we have a better platform that can do this for us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Today, with the crowd-sourcing platforms, when people put their prices there, you can do an instant comparison.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I think this is even more effective in deterring those merchants that may be pricing their goods unfairly.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, in Yishun, our favourite constituency, supposing we can set up an area to tell people where in Yishun is the cheapest coffee, the cheapest kaya toast and, if your residents can access the information easily and people can freely put and make available the prices that they are offering in Yishun, then it will help consumers to stretch their hard-earned dollar; and it will be a much faster process than trying to submit a coffee price increase to someone else and come back later in that process.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: In this open and transparent platform, I think it will help to deter those people who may want to price their products that is out of the norm.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is why I asked to work with NTUC and CASE to proliferate or promote this platform so that we can get a faster response time.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Surely, as the Member said, we do not want the situation where for one coffee shop, we send the matter to CASE then wait for two weeks and come back with the result.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And you also want a certain deterrent effect that people do not spread false rumours.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: For example, what the Member has suggested, some people said that "I am increasing my price because of the GST hike", but the GST hike is not even coming in yet and not for a few years' time!

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, that is obviously not the right reason that they do what they are doing.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I hope that through such open platform and open sharing, we can have a faster response to some of these ground issues.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Last but not least, I hope I am not stealing the thunder from the Member Mr Seah Kian Peng.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is a common question which I have always been asked: "Why is it that, once in a while, NTUC, as a social enterprise, has other companies which beat their prices?" On behalf of Mr Seah Kian Peng, from what I understand from him, NTUC FairPrice has a basket of 500 items.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But that does not mean that every item is 4%-5% below the market price.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: On the other hand, if we study marketing, we will also know that from part of the sales strategy, it is in my interest as a competitor to NTUC FairPrice to make sure that, every day, I have a few items below NTUC's prices, in order to attract people to go there because, when you are there, you would not just buy the few items that are on discount.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: This is quite common in the Fast-Moving Consumer Goods (FMCG) market.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Having said that, I am quite sure NTUC FairPrice will be working very hard to source from multiple agencies to try and reduce the prices, including the recent effort on milk powder, the number of house brands as they continue to expand their products and so forth.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, I think that is the commitment of NTUC.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One very interesting question that I have always wondered in my mind is not so much whether Sheng Siong or Dairy Farm is able to meet and beat NTUC prices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The question is that, if we do not have social enterprises to benchmark some of these things, would the other competitors still charge those prices?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That was actually the story of the "Welcome Supermarket" in the 1970s.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It was not that they just meet or try to beat NTUC prices once in a while, but it was because of the benchmark.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In terms of the impact of economic forces, such as the interest rate outlook, going forward, what will be the Minister's view on that, because with the Fed probably raising rates, it would have an impact on Singaporeans in terms of cash outlay in the future, and what is probably the transmission mechanism, taking into consideration our exchange rate policy regime, but what will be the impact of the interest rate outlook going forward and the impact on Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Yesterday, when we talked about the impact of the trade wars, I briefly mentioned this.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If, because of the trade wars and because of the interest hike, it leads to an overall dampening of the global confidence level and people's investment, then what affects us most severely is job creation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If we cannot continue to create good jobs for our people, the rest of these other help schemes are actually secondary because, first and foremost, we must have good jobs for our people.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: When our economy grows, our people have jobs and we have the means to help one another by redistributing some of the gains from this entire economic system.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But if the economy shrinks because of the downturn in global market confidence, then there is a significant impact.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, there are three levels of impact: (a) the direct interest rate cost that the Member mentioned on business; (b) the impact on the exchange rate which affects our ability to contain imported inflation; (c) and most importantly, and together with the headwinds that we face in the global trading environment, how it affects our economy and our ability to continue to create good jobs for our people to earn good incomes.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I just have a few questions for the Minister.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Indeed, the cost of living is a big issue, and the eight-pronged approach that he has outlined, the strategies, are all very important.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I just want to say that, in addition, one key aspect – perhaps, it is within the eight but I did not hear it – is about consumer education.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Frankly, I think all of us know that eating-in is a lot cheaper than eating-out, wherever you may go.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: So, things like that may be simple tips.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But I think they are useful tips which could be incorporated within the eight tips that the Minister has.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Speaking as an employer, too, the cost of doing business is, indeed, something which needs to be addressed.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I know the Minister has outlined some of them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In the case of at least my business at NTUC FairPrice – labour, rent and utilities – these are the three biggest cost levers.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: On utilities, we all look forward to the opening up of the electricity market that will help all businesses and individuals alike.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: But on the part of labour and rent, these are areas which the Government is in a position to see how it can continue to effect a dampening of that.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: During the tea break later, I will explain to Er Dr Lee Bee Wah on some of the things she raised.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I will fill her in on other details.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: My final point is that I am wearing the hat – again declaring my interest – as Chief Executive Officer (CEO) of NTUC FairPrice and also part of the NTUC Enterprise network.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I think the Minister's eight strategies about leveraging social enterprises is something that the NTUC Group and the NTUC Enterprises will certainly be keen to work on and to play our part in seeing how, as a group, we can address this very important issue for all of us.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: First, consumer education is my strategy No 7.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why we work closely with CASE to enable consumer choices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We are not here to judge whether somebody should buy this or buy that and what should be necessary for your particular lifestyle.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: If you can afford it and want to do it, by all means.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I think our job is to enable consumer choice through consumer education.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Let us take the recent example of milk powder.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I was the one who sent Mr Seah Kian Peng – I think he still has the photo.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One day, when I was shopping at NTUC FairPrice, I was very perturbed because when I walked down the food aisles, the only food item, single item that costs more than $100 for some of the products was milk powder.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Why is it that milk powder – same size, same volume – can cost $30-something, $80-something and $120?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I took a photo and sent it to Mr Seah Kian Peng and I asked him which is the most popular brand, that means, from sales.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And I was very puzzled what is the difference between the $30 brand, $80 brand and $120 brand?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, the $120 brand was because some children might be allergic to some ingredients and that is why there is a special formulation.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Then what about the $30 brand versus the $80 brand?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: I asked Mr Seah Kian Peng if he could bring in more of the $30 brand.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: They have tried before but it did not sell well.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Maybe because we will always want the best for our children and we wonder should we stinge on that $50 extra for one can of milk powder.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And we ask, "What if there are real benefits which my child is not getting?" We can understand that kind of psychology.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But, over time, through consumer education, we have been able to expand the market share of the $30-plus brand, including some of the house brands that NTUC FairPrice has brought in.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But today, if I am not wrong, the $80-plus brand is still the most popular range segment.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: It has come down but it is still quite high.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That shows that, actually, all of us can play our part to assure family members of the quality of the products.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: And NTUC FairPrice has a lot of house brands.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But, again, when I was the NTUC Secretary-General, they would not always sell the most or be the most popular brand.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: Last but not least, we thank NTUC Enterprises for continuing to show leadership in the pricing of its many products and services beyond groceries today, including healthcare, eldercare and also childcare.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: I was hoping Minister Chan would also say something about CASE, but he only defended NTUC FairPrice!

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: So, if I may just clarify for the hon Member for Yishun, to provide feedback, you do not need to be a member of CASE.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: You only need to be a member of CASE if you want CASE to represent the consumer to liaise with the business.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan (Mountbatten)
text: On the point made by the Member Er Dr Lee Bee Wah that complaining to CASE has no effect because price —

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: — that you do not want the consumer to go to CASE because price has gone up.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: The reality, as Minister Chan has mentioned, is that every business has different price pressures.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: So, their rental may be more expensive because they are in a better locality, they may have to pay more for their staff.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: So, CASE finds it very difficult really to be able to decide which business is profiteering because it sets higher prices.

speaker: Mr Lim Biow Chuan
text: So, thank you, Mr Speaker, for allowing me to raise that clarification on behalf of CASE.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: I did not say that it is not effective to bring the matter to CASE.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: What I meant is that the cost of living or the profiteering issue affects every Singaporean.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: We do not want every Singaporean to go to CASE, same as we do not want every o-Bike victim to go to CASE, because it would be flooded by all these cases.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah
text: We would like MTI to set up a committee to look into specific cases because if one stall increases its price by 50 cents, the next day, another stall will also increase its price by 50 cents.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah, you can settle with Mr Seah Kian Peng and Mr Lim Biow Chuan later at tea.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I brought up this issue during the Opening of the Second Session of this Parliament.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I think a lot of businesses, because they signed short leases of three years, every time the lease is due for renewal, they face a big surprise from the landlord saying the rental going forward would increase by a huge amount and, if they do not renew, they would have to reinstate.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The landlord is actually using this friction of having to incur reinstatement costs to their advantage.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: All these actually feed into the cost of living because the businesses suffer the higher costs on renewal of rental rates and, because of that, they have to charge consumers higher.

speaker: Mr Yee Chia Hsing (Chua Chu Kang)
text: So, I hope MTI will look into my suggestions of having longer lease periods as well as mandating that landlords should not put their reinstatement "clause" into all their tenancy contracts.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But we accept the point and I think Mr Yee Chia Hsing has made the point during the Committee of Supply that the contract must be fair to both sides, and I think that is something that we will certainly encourage and look into.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But I think we cannot mandate every lease to be of a certain length because the businesses also require certain flexibility because of their different business models.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But in all these things, we will have to strike a balance between protecting the consumer and facilitating the business and innovative practices, especially in the current era whereby there is a proliferation of new business models, including the ones that the Member has mentioned.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We will have to strike the right balance to make sure that we protect our consumers and yet, at the same time, not stifle innovative practices.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: We have to find a balancing point as we continue to go along.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I know it is published based on income groups, but there could be other demographic groups, such as the three groups where the Government has presented its measures, for example, young couples, parents with young children, and retirees.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Government consider publishing a CPI based on these groups because there could be certain factors, for instance, price of milk powder could be one example, which affect certain groups by demographic characteristics, rather than just by income characteristics, and that may enable us to have more well-informed debates about policy?

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: So, as Members can see from the charts, we do have various ways to look at the data differently.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: One dimension would be by income, the bottom 20th percentile, the middle 60th and the top 20th percentile.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: The other dimension that Mr Leon Perera mentioned, for example, is retirees, because they generally have no income from work and may be living on their savings.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: That is why MTI started monitoring the data.

speaker: Mr Chan Chun Sing
text: But it takes us some time to build up by different demographic groups, and we will make available those data when we have them.
